title: Is Rs 5 Crore Enough to Retire in India or Do You Need Rs 10 Crore
excerpt: Retirement planning in India increasingly revolves around viral corpus targets, but financial experts say the right number depends on lifestyle, location, and inflation — not social media benchmarks.
body:
• For couples with moderate expenses and no major loans, a well-structured Rs 4-5 crore corpus can sustain a 30-year retirement
  • Metro dwellers spending Rs 2 lakh or more per month may need Rs 8-10 crore to maintain their lifestyle through retirement
  • At 6% inflation, Rs 1 lakh in monthly expenses today could become Rs 5.7 lakh in 30 years, making inflation the biggest variable in retirement math
  • Financial planners stress starting from actual monthly expenses, not viral social media corpus targets

Every few months, a new retirement corpus number starts trending across Indian social media and personal finance forums. Rs 10 crore. Rs 15 crore. Rs 20 crore. The numbers keep climbing, and the message is usually the same: unless you accumulate a massive corpus, retirement will be a struggle.

But a growing chorus of financial planners and research teams says the fixation on a single large number is misleading — and potentially harmful to sound planning.

The Myth of the Universal Retirement Number

The idea that every Indian household needs Rs 10 crore or Rs 20 crore to retire comfortably is one of the most persistent myths in personal finance. A retired couple living in Jaipur with a paid-off home and monthly expenses of Rs 60,000 will need a fundamentally different corpus from a couple in Mumbai spending Rs 2 lakh a month on rent, travel, and premium healthcare.

"What most investors get wrong is that they start with the corpus and then try to fit their retirement around it. The correct approach is the opposite. First define the life you want after retirement. The corpus requirement emerges from that exercise."

— Sanjiv Bajaj, Joint Chairman and MD, Bajaj Capital

Retirement adequacy depends on five core variables: monthly expenses, retirement age, life expectancy, inflation, and expected portfolio returns during retirement. Change any one of these, and the required corpus shifts dramatically.

When Rs 5 Crore Can Work

For a couple retiring in their early 50s with no dependent children, no major loans, and a fully paid-off home, a Rs 5 crore corpus can be sufficient — provided it is structured properly. A couple spending Rs 90,000 to Rs 1 lakh a month in retirement would need roughly Rs 12-16 lakh annually. Against a Rs 5 crore portfolio, that translates to a first-year withdrawal rate of about 3.2%, well within the range most financial planners consider sustainable.

A sample retirement portfolio structure at this level might allocate 45% (Rs 2.25 crore) to bonds and fixed-income products yielding around 8% annually, 40% (Rs 2 crore) to diversified equity index funds for long-term inflation protection, and 15% (Rs 75 lakh) to fixed deposits for emergency liquidity. The bond portion alone could generate roughly Rs 1.33 lakh per month before tax, covering regular expenses without forcing equity sales during a market downturn.

When You Need Rs 8-10 Crore

The Rs 5 crore plan starts to strain for households with higher spending. A couple spending Rs 2 lakh a month — Rs 24 lakh a year — would face a first-year withdrawal rate of 4.8% on a Rs 5 crore corpus, leaving thin margins for inflation, taxes, and healthcare emergencies.

At 6% annual inflation, that Rs 2 lakh monthly expense becomes roughly Rs 3.6 lakh in 10 years. For couples in metro cities who prioritize frequent travel, premium healthcare, and a high-end lifestyle, Rs 8 crore to Rs 10 crore becomes a more realistic target. At a 3.5% withdrawal rate, Rs 8 crore supports Rs 28 lakh in annual withdrawals, while Rs 10 crore supports Rs 35 lakh — providing substantially more breathing room.

The Inflation Factor

The most underestimated variable in retirement planning is inflation's compounding effect over a 30-year horizon. A monthly expense of Rs 1 lakh today could erode to a purchasing power equivalent of just Rs 17 lakh in today's terms over 30 years at 6% inflation. Alternatively, maintaining the same lifestyle would require nearly Rs 5.7 lakh per month three decades from now.

This is precisely why financial planners emphasize that even retirees need growth assets in their portfolio. A couple retiring at 52 may need their corpus to last until their mid-80s — a 30-plus year horizon. Moving everything into fixed deposits at retirement may feel safe, but the portfolio risks losing real value year after year.

The Right Question to Ask

The emerging consensus among financial planners is that the debate between Rs 5 crore and Rs 10 crore misses the point entirely. The right starting point is not a viral target but a clear-eyed assessment of actual monthly expenses, the city you plan to retire in, healthcare needs, and whether dependents remain in the picture.

For many Indian households — particularly those with controlled spending, no major liabilities, and a willingness to live outside the most expensive metros — a well-managed Rs 4-5 crore portfolio with the right mix of bonds, index funds, and emergency liquidity can sustain a comfortable retirement. For others, particularly in Mumbai or Bengaluru with premium lifestyles, Rs 10 crore may be the floor rather than the ceiling.

The discipline lies not in reaching an arbitrary number, but in stress-testing whatever corpus you have against your own inflation-adjusted expenses — and reviewing it periodically as healthcare costs, tax policy, and market returns evolve.
nri_angle: NRIs planning to return to India or retire there face similar corpus planning challenges, with metro vs tier-2 city choices significantly affecting required savings.
